transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me today. I really appreciate it. Um... I hope I do a good job explaining this, I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information. 

I've been having a little trouble at work—I'm a mechanic—and... well, I really don't want you to think badly of me, but I keep hearing this man's voice. It usually comes from the garage vents, or sometimes right from under the hood when I'm working on a vehicle. It's so clear, just exactly like somebody is standing right next to me. 

He keeps telling me... well, he tells me not to trust my husband. And he tells me not to touch certain cars in the shop. I know that probably sounds really strange, doesn't it? I promise I'm trying my best to handle it, but I just thought maybe I should talk to someone. Am I making sense?
How long have you been hearing this voice? When did it first start?

Um... well, I really hope I didn't wait too long to come in. I just didn't want to make a big deal out of nothing, or be a bother to anyone, you know? But... gosh, I guess it's been about ten months now. That's when the voice first started. 

And, um, I guess around that same time, I started having these... well, these worries that I was being tracked. I know how terrible that sounds, I really do. I've tried so hard to just keep my head down and work through it on my own so I wouldn't let anybody down. 

Is that... I mean, is ten months a really bad sign? I hope you're not upset with me that I waited so long to get help. I really am trying my best.

Over these past ten months, have there been periods where you felt unusually sad or depressed, or conversely, periods where you felt unusually energetic, excited, or like you needed very little sleep?

Um... well, I hope I'm answering this the way you need me to. I try really hard not to get too down or sad, I always try to look on the bright side so I'm not a burden to anyone. But, um... as for the energy part... I guess there have been times where I really didn't need much rest at all. 

For weeks at a time, actually, I'd sleep maybe two or three hours a night. I'd wake up way before dawn, and my mind would already be right there in the garage, thinking about the vehicles and what I needed to fix. I just felt like sleeping any more would just waste time, you know? I wanted to be productive and get a head start. 

I mean, being a hard worker is a good thing, right? I really hope you don't think I was being irresponsible with my health by not sleeping... I just genuinely felt like I didn't need it. Does that answer your question okay?

When you were sleeping only a few hours a night and feeling that energy and productivity, were you also experiencing periods of feeling unusually happy, excited, or elevated in your mood—or was it more just about having the energy and motivation to work?

Um... well, I want to be completely honest with you, even though I'm a little embarrassed to admit this next part. I really don't want you to think I'm a bad person. 

But yes, I did feel really happy during those times. Actually, I'd be flying high, just feeling so incredibly good, like I could fix every single car in town all by myself. It felt like a positive thing at first, you know? Being that motivated and confident. 

But... gosh, I feel terrible saying this because I really try to be kind to everyone... my mood would sometimes just snap. Like, if I was in that zone and my husband just asked a simple question about why the dishes weren't done, or if one of the other techs at the shop just moved my socket set... I would just blow up. I'd get so angry, like they were purposely trying to hold me down or ruin my momentum. 

I always feel so guilty about it afterward, because I really am not a mean person, I promise. I don't want you to think I'm a bad wife or a difficult coworker. I just get so wrapped up in doing a good job. Is it... I mean, is it okay that I get a little snappy like that when I'm just trying to work hard? I hope you can understand where I'm coming from.

When you're having those periods where you feel normal—not the high-energy times and not feeling down—do you still hear that man's voice and have those worries about being tracked, or do those experiences only happen when you're in that energetic, elevated mood state?

Um... well... I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information, so I'll try my best to explain. 

Even when I'm feeling a bit more... normal, I guess? Like, there was a quieter few weeks recently where I was actually sleeping a normal amount, and I wasn't making all those huge plans for the shop or feeling all that high energy. I was just trying to be a good, steady worker and a good wife. 

But... oh gosh, I hope you don't think I'm completely losing my mind... even during those quiet weeks, I still heard that man's voice in the garage. And... I still really believed that my husband and my boss were tracking me. 

I really tried to ignore it, I promise I did. I didn't want to cause any trouble or make a fuss. But it was still there, even when I wasn't feeling all revved up. Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it right. I just want to be a good patient and give you the answers you need.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F25.1 (schizoaffective disorder, depressive type). Patient demonstrates clear manic/hypomanic episodes with decreased need for sleep, elevated mood, increased goal-directed activity, and irritability. Psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions) persist even during euthymic periods, but are most prominent during mood elevation. This pattern is most consistent with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.0) rather than depressive type.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a 10-month history of psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and delusions of being tracked) that persist during both elevated mood states and euthymic periods, combined with distinct episodes of decreased need for sleep, elevated/expansive mood, irritability, and increased goal-directed activity. The key distinguishing feature is that psychotic symptoms are NOT confined to mood episodes—they persist during normal mood periods—which is pathognomonic for schizoaffective disorder rather than bipolar disorder with psychotic features or primary psychosis. This pattern of mood episodes with concurrent but independent psychotic symptoms meets F25.0 (Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type).

Delusion of persecution: belief that husband and boss are tracking her
Psychotic symptoms persist during euthymic periods (quieter weeks with normal sleep)
Decreased need for sleep: sleeping 2-3 hours per night for weeks at a time
Early morning awakening with immediate goal-directed thinking about work
Elevated/expansive mood: feeling 'flying high,' incredibly good, confident she could fix every car in town
Increased goal-directed activity: heightened productivity and work motivation
Irritability: mood snapping, explosive anger at minor provocations (husband's questions, coworker moving tools)

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Psychotic symptoms and mood disturbance present for 10 months; manic episodes occurred in weeks-long periods within this timeframe; psychotic symptoms confirmed to persist during euthymic periods as well.
additional_requirements: Psychotic symptoms present during both elevated mood episodes and euthymic periods (not mood-congruent only)
Distinct episodes of manic/hypomanic features with decreased need for sleep, elevated mood, and irritability
Functional impairment at work (trouble at work, impaired work performance) and in relationships (guilt about anger toward husband)
